reference.source: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
clinicalPearls: A limb-threatening emergency caused by massive proximal (iliofemoral) deep vein thrombosis with near-total venous outflow obstruction
Classic triad of severe pain, extensive oedema, and cyanosis (blue discolouration) of the affected limb
Often preceded by phlegmasia alba dolens, a pale, swollen limb, as thrombosis progresses to occlude collaterals
Massive venous congestion raises compartment pressure, compromises arterial inflow, and can progress to venous gangrene and compartment syndrome
Frequently associated with an underlying prothrombotic state, particularly malignancy, and may cause substantial fluid sequestration and circulatory compromise

Requires urgent anticoagulation, limb elevation, and fluid resuscitation, with catheter-directed thrombolysis or thrombectomy to restore venous outflow in appropriate patients; fasciotomy may be needed for compartment syndrome
Carries a high risk of pulmonary embolism and of significant limb loss and mortality
reference.pathophysiology: Phlegmasia cerulea dolens is the extreme of iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis, in which thrombus occludes not only the major deep veins but also the collateral channels, producing near-complete venous outflow obstruction. The resulting massive rise in interstitial and venous pressure causes gross oedema and cyanosis, and can exceed capillary and eventually arterial perfusion pressure, leading to ischaemia, venous gangrene, and compartment syndrome. Large volumes of fluid sequester in the limb, causing hypovolaemia and shock. An underlying hypercoagulable state, often malignancy, is common.
additionalDifferentials: Acute arterial occlusion or acute limb ischaemia
additionalInvestigations: Venous duplex ultrasound to confirm extensive proximal thrombosis
CT or MR venography to define the extent and any iliac compression or obstruction
Assessment of limb perfusion and compartment pressures where ischaemia is suspected
Investigation for underlying malignancy or thrombophilia
Baseline coagulation and renal function before thrombolysis
Chest imaging or CT pulmonary angiography if pulmonary embolism is suspected
redFlags: Progression to venous gangrene or absent arterial signals, indicating a threatened limb
Haemodynamic compromise from fluid sequestration or massive pulmonary embolism
Rapidly advancing cyanosis and pain despite anticoagulation
reference.prognosis: A serious emergency with significant risk of limb loss, pulmonary embolism, and death; prompt anticoagulation and thrombus removal can salvage the limb, but venous gangrene carries a poor outcome and any underlying malignancy influences survival.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for acute arterial ischaemia and delaying anticoagulation
Underestimating fluid sequestration and failing to resuscitate
Delaying thrombolysis or thrombectomy until gangrene has developed
references: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
ESVS Clinical Practice Guidelines on Venous Disease
management: Institute emergency therapeutic anticoagulation with intravenous unfractionated heparin as the immediate priority
Give aggressive fluid resuscitation for hypovolaemia and shock and elevate the limb to reduce venous congestion
Restore venous outflow urgently with catheter-directed thrombolysis or venous thrombectomy in suitable patients
Perform fasciotomy for compartment syndrome and debride or amputate established venous gangrene
Investigate and treat an underlying prothrombotic state, particularly occult malignancy or thrombophilia
Monitor for and manage concurrent pulmonary embolism
Escalate immediately to vascular surgery and critical care for this limb- and life-threatening emergency
